content: Chickenpox, also known as varicella, is a highly contagious disease caused by the varicella-zoster virus (VZV). It is characterized by an itchy rash, fever, and fatigue, and can lead to serious complications in some cases. The disease spreads through respiratory droplets or direct contact with the fluid from chickenpox blisters. The U.S. chickenpox vaccination program has significantly reduced the incidence of the disease over the past 25 years. The vaccine is highly effective in preventing chickenpox and its complications. It is recommended for children, adolescents, and adults who have not had the disease or been vaccinated previously. The vaccine schedule and its importance are outlined in detail to ensure proper immunization. Healthcare professionals are provided with clinical guidelines on chickenpox prevention, including strategies for healthcare settings, criteria for evidence of immunity, and the use of the varicella vaccine. Routine vaccine recommendations, considerations for specific populations, and evidence supporting immunity are also available for medical practitioners. Laboratory testing for the varicella-zoster virus is essential for confirming cases of chickenpox and shingles. Detailed instructions are provided for collecting and shipping specimens for VZV testing, along with information on obtaining appropriate supplies. Clinical guidance is available for managing patients at high risk of severe chickenpox, including immunocompromised individuals and pregnant women. Surveillance and reporting systems are in place to monitor varicella cases, deaths, and outbreaks. The CDC collaborates with state health departments to control and respond to varicella outbreaks effectively.
